title: BMRCL Rejects Calls to Cut Namma Metro Fares, Says Fare Fixation Committee's Recommendations Are Binding
text:
News Brief
Arjun Brij
Dec 04, 2025, 10:06 AM | Updated 10:06 AM IST
Save & read from anywhere!
Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app.
Bangalore Metro Rail Corporation Limited (BMRCL) has confirmed that it will not reconsider the revised Namma Metro fares, despite sustained criticism from mobility experts, commuters and several elected leaders.
Times of India reported that in a formal response to Bangalore South MP Tejasvi Surya, the corporation reiterated that it is obligated to follow the recommendations of the Fare Fixation Committee (FFC), describing them as binding.
The clarification comes months after BMRCL increased fares sharply in February, triggering widespread pushback.
The initial revision saw fares rise by as much as 110 per cent, prompting the corporation to rework the structure and limit the highest increase to 71 per cent. Even with the adjustment, Namma Metro remains the most expensive metro service in India.
By comparison, Delhi Metro’s recent fare revision was far lower, with changes of only Re 1 to Rs 4 depending on distance.
For longer commutes, the difference is more pronounced — Namma Metro now charges Rs 90 for trips over 25 km, while Delhi Metro collects Rs 64 for distances beyond 32 km.
In its letter, BMRCL defended the revised structure, arguing that global metro systems depend heavily on farebox revenue to sustain operations and maintenance.
It stated that non-fare earnings, such as advertising and property-related income, cannot replace passenger revenue, noting that metro stations offer limited commercial opportunities.
As the corporation wrote, “A metro system is a transit service, not a terminal facility… Commercial opportunities within Metro stations are naturally constrained.”
Addressing concerns about the financial methodology used, BMRCL said that the 2017 fare revision was based on audited data from FY 2016–17, when Phase 1 became fully operational.
Under FFC rules, subsequent revisions must use the same base year to ensure consistency.
It also clarified that the cited 366 per cent rise in maintenance and administration costs reflects accumulated index-based movement over 7.5 years, not a direct comparison of audited costs, adding that the two measures “cannot be equated.”
BMRCL noted that although FFC recommendations allowed increases of up to 81.8 per cent across slabs, it moderated the rollout after testing more than 600 combinations, ultimately capping the highest hike at 71.4 per cent.
